subChunks.title: CAP Theorem, Consistency Models & Failure Modes
subChunks.hookHtml: The moment your system spans more than one process, you have entered distributed systems territory — where network partitions, clock skew, and partial failures are not edge cases but the normal operating environment. Understanding CAP theorem and failure modes is what separates engineers who design robust systems from those who are surprised when things break.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
CAP Theorem

In a distributed system, you can guarantee at most two of three properties during a network partition:

  • Consistency (C): every read returns the most recent write or an error (all nodes see the same data at the same time)
  • Availability (A): every request receives a response (not necessarily the latest data)
  • Partition Tolerance (P): the system continues operating despite network partitions

Since network partitions are inevitable in any real distributed system, you always have P. The real choice is CP (consistent but may be unavailable during partition) vs AP (always available but may return stale data during partition).

Examples: CP — HBase, ZooKeeper, traditional RDBMS with synchronous replication. AP — Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB.

Consistency Models

  • Strong consistency: reads always see the latest write. Requires coordination (consensus). High latency.
  • Eventual consistency: all replicas will converge to the same value — eventually. Reads may be stale during the convergence window.
  • Read-your-writes: a user always sees their own writes reflected immediately (even if others may not).
  • Causal consistency: if A caused B, every observer sees A before B.

Common Failure Modes

  • Node failure: a process crashes. Detectable via heartbeat timeout.
  • Network partition: nodes cannot communicate. They each think the other has failed.
  • Split-brain: two nodes believe they are the leader. Leads to data divergence. Prevented by quorum consensus (majority must agree).
  • Byzantine failure: a node sends incorrect or malicious data. Requires Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) — expensive and rare in private systems.

Distributed System Patterns

Two-phase commit (2PC): coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then commit or abort. Provides distributed atomicity but blocks if coordinator fails. Avoid in high-throughput systems.

Saga pattern: break a distributed transaction into local transactions with compensating actions for rollback. Each service commits locally; failures trigger compensation. No blocking coordinator.

Idempotency: an operation that produces the same result whether applied once or many times. Critical in distributed systems where retries are common — payment deduplication by idempotency key is the standard example.

// Simulating eventual consistency with in-memory replicas
Map<String, String> primary   = new HashMap<>();
Map<String, String> secondary = new HashMap<>();

// Write to primary
primary.put("user:1", "Lyria");
// Async replication — secondary is briefly stale
new Thread(() -> {
    try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    secondary.put("user:1", primary.get("user:1"));
}).start();

// Stale read from secondary before replication completes
System.out.println(secondary.get("user:1")); // null — eventual consistency window

storyBeats.text: The Academy's multi-continent replica cluster had two Guild Masters — one in the East tower, one in the West. The network between them went down for 30 seconds. Both towers continued accepting write requests. When the partition healed, 47 spells had conflicting versions. This was the day the Academy learned what CAP theorem costs in production.

storyBeats.speaker: Distributed Systems Lead Kova
storyBeats.text: CAP theorem is not theoretical — it is a constraint you live with every day. You must choose: do we refuse requests during a partition to preserve consistency, or do we answer with potentially stale data to preserve availability? Neither is wrong. But you must decide consciously, not accidentally.

storyBeats.speaker: Distributed Systems Lead Kova
storyBeats.text: Split-brain is the nightmare. Two nodes both think they are the primary, both accept writes. When the partition heals, you have two divergent histories. The solution is a quorum: you can only elect a leader if more than half the nodes agree. A minority partition gets no leader — it becomes unavailable rather than inconsistent. That is the CP choice.

storyBeats.speaker: Idempotency key pattern
Distributed Systems Lead Kova
storyBeats.text: Eventual consistency does not mean 'it might be wrong forever.' It means 'during the convergence window, you might see a slightly stale value — but the system will catch up.' For most reads — user profile, product catalogue, feed items — this is perfectly acceptable. For financial balances and inventory counts, you probably want stronger guarantees.

learningObjectives: Explain the CAP theorem and why partition tolerance makes CP vs AP the real trade-off
Distinguish between strong consistency, eventual consistency, and read-your-writes consistency
Describe split-brain and explain how quorum consensus prevents it
Define idempotency and explain why it is essential in distributed systems with retries
commonMistakes: Choosing AP or CP without understanding the consistency requirements of each operation type
Treating eventual consistency as 'possibly wrong forever' — it converges; the question is how quickly
Using two-phase commit for high-throughput distributed transactions — saga pattern is more appropriate
Not making retryable operations idempotent — double charges, duplicate records result
assessmentCriteria: Can classify a given database (e.g. ZooKeeper, Cassandra) as CP or AP and explain the implication
Can describe what happens during a network partition for a CP system vs an AP system
Can explain why idempotency keys prevent double-processing on retry with a code example
Can describe the saga pattern and name one advantage over two-phase commit
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the CAP theorem to a developer building their first multi-node system. What does it mean in practice when choosing a database? Give a concrete example of a CP trade-off and an AP trade-off in the same application.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write a DistributedDemo class that simulates eventual consistency between two in-memory maps:

  1. Write a method void writeWithDelay(Map<String,String> primary, Map<String,String> replica, String key, String value, long delayMs) that writes to primary immediately and replicates to replica after delayMs milliseconds using a new Thread.
  2. In main: call writeWithDelay with key='spell:1', value='Fireball', delay=100ms
  3. Immediately read from both primary and replica (replica will be null — stale read)
  4. Sleep 200ms, then read from replica again — it should be 'Fireball' by then
  5. Print both pre-sleep and post-sleep replica reads
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Write a class IdempotentPayment that simulates an idempotency key payment processor:

  • Use a Map<String, String> processedKeys to store idempotencyKey → result
  • Write method String processPayment(String idempotencyKey, int amount) that returns the cached result if the key already exists, otherwise 'processes' the payment (just returns 'paid:'+amount) and stores the result
  • In main: call it twice with the same key 'txn-001' and amount 500. Confirm the result is 'paid:500' both times but only 'processed once' (add a print inside the processing path)
  • Call once with a different key 'txn-002' and verify it processes

soloPracticeTests.label: Second call with same key returns cached result
Only processed once for duplicate key

questions.questionHtml: In the CAP theorem, if partition tolerance (P) is always required in a real distributed system, what is the actual trade-off a designer must make?
options: Between consistency (C) and availability (A) during a network partition
questions.correctAnswer: Between consistency (C) and availability (A) during a network partition
questions.explanationHtml: Network partitions are inevitable, so P must always be tolerated. The real choice is: during a partition, does the system refuse requests to preserve consistency (CP), or continue serving requests with potentially stale data (AP)? Both are valid depending on your consistency requirements.

questions.questionHtml: A payment service retries failed API calls. Without idempotency keys, what is the risk?
options: The payment may be charged twice if the first request succeeded but the response was lost
The retry will be slower than the first attempt
The service will run out of database connections
questions.correctAnswer: The payment may be charged twice if the first request succeeded but the response was lost
questions.explanationHtml: Network failures can occur after the server processes the request but before the client receives the response. Without idempotency, the client retries and the server processes again — resulting in a double charge. Idempotency keys let the server recognise the retry and return the original result without reprocessing.

questions.questionHtml: Two nodes in a cluster both believe they are the leader after a network partition. What is this called and how does quorum consensus prevent it?
options: Split-brain — prevented by requiring majority agreement (quorum) to elect a leader
Cascade failure — prevented by circuit breakers
questions.correctAnswer: Split-brain — prevented by requiring majority agreement (quorum) to elect a leader
questions.explanationHtml: Split-brain occurs when a network partition causes two nodes to independently believe they are the leader. Quorum consensus (Raft, Paxos) requires that a leader can only be elected if more than half the nodes agree. A minority partition cannot reach quorum, so it loses leadership and becomes unavailable rather than allowing two simultaneous leaders.
